report:
## Conclusion

The evidence is mixed, and current high-quality data suggest that any benefit is small at best and highly uncertain overall.

Earlier meta-analyses (e.g., Cochrane's 2010 update) reported that probiotics, especially certain *Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG* strains, could modestly shorten diarrhea duration (by roughly ~1 day) and reduce stool frequency. However, the updated 2020 Cochrane systematic review (82 trials, >12,000 participants, mostly children) revised this conclusion: it found that probiotics "probably make little or no difference" to the proportion of people with diarrhea lasting ≥48 hours, and it is now **uncertain** whether probiotics meaningfully shorten diarrhea duration, largely due to substantial heterogeneity among trials, strain differences, and risk of bias in the underlying studies (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea; https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub4/information).

This reassessment was reinforced by two large, rigorous, multi-center U.S. randomized controlled trials published in the New England Journal of Medicine (2018), which tested *L. rhamnosus GG* and a combination probiotic in children with acute gastroenteritis presenting to emergency departments. Neither trial found any significant difference from placebo in diarrhea duration, severity, or other outcomes (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802598).

**Bottom line:** While probiotics are generally safe and some older, smaller studies suggested modest reductions in diarrhea duration, the best current evidence—an updated Cochrane review and large well-designed RCTs—indicates that any benefit is uncertain or minimal, and probiotics should not be considered a reliably effective treatment for shortening acute infectious diarrhea. Rehydration remains the cornerstone of treatment.
